# sv0c/sv0vm: raw pointers, real `unsafe` blocks, and an FFI/exact-ABI contract

## purpose

Resolve **OQ-007** (the open sv0 FFI/ABI contract question), unblocking
`sv0-strings` **SS-203** (exact C ABI manifest + unsafe caller obligations,
BL-103) and **SS-204** (feature-gated raw C ABI + external linkage tests,
BL-104) — together, `strings_unsafe_abi`, which today is entirely unimplemented
(`lib/strings_unsafe_abi.sv0`'s own docstring: *"Status: not started — gated
behind an accepted sv0 FFI/ABI contract"*). This is also the prerequisite any
other sv0 package would need to call a real C library, so it belongs at the
language/toolchain level, not inside `sv0-strings`.

**This is a genuinely larger effort than it first looks** — the grounding audit
below found that `unsafe` and raw pointers, despite being *documented* in
`sv0doc` as language features, are **not actually implemented**. This doc is
scoped like an M4/M5-sized feature area (multiple epics, phased, scope
decisions to lock up front) rather than a single Track U slice, because that is
what the real gap turns out to be.

## grounding audit (2026-09-14)

**What `sv0doc` documents** (`sv0doc/memory-model/ownership.md` §8.4-8.5,
`sv0doc/type-system/rules.md` §3.3): `*const T` / `*mut T` raw pointer types;
creating one is safe, dereferencing requires `unsafe`; raw pointers don't
participate in the borrow checker; stated purposes include kernel/hardware
access and **FFI with C libraries**.

**What `sv0c` actually implements** (source-verified, not doc-inferred — the
same "verify against code" discipline this project's own memory already flags
for the sibling `impl Trait for T` operator-overload gap):

- `unsafe` **is** a lexed keyword (`lexer.sv0` token 93) and **is** parsed —
  but only as an **optional modifier before a function declaration**
  (`ps_skip_optional_unsafe`, `is_unsafe_token`). It is accepted syntactically
  (`pub unsafe fn foo()`) and then **discarded** — no semantic effect, no
  checker rule references it, and **there is no `unsafe { ... }` block-expression
  form at all**. `grep -rn unsafe sv0c/lib/checker.sv0` returns nothing.
- `Ty` (`sv0c/lib/ast.sv0`) has `TyRef`, `TyRefMut`, `TyArray` — **no
  `TyPtr`/`TyRaw` variant exists**. Raw pointer types cannot even be named in
  source today; there is nothing for the parser to produce or the checker to
  validate.
- There is **no `extern` keyword, no FFI declaration syntax, and no
  exact-signature/calling-convention machinery** anywhere in the lexer, parser,
  or checker.
- The C backend already *is* real C — every sv0 function is emitted as an
  ordinary C function with the platform's default calling convention, so the
  C-backend half of "exact ABI" is largely already true by construction; what's
  missing is a **declared, checked contract** for calling *external* C symbols
  (a function the compiler didn't emit) and for a raw-pointer type to pass
  through that boundary.
- The VM backend has **no equivalent capability whatsoever**: `sv0vm` is a
  pure bytecode interpreter over its own value representation; there is no
  notion of a raw memory address, no foreign-call opcode, and no marshaling
  layer between VM values and a C ABI.

**Conclusion**: OQ-007 is not "write down a contract for an existing capability
and ship a feature flag." It is: design and implement raw pointer types end to
end (parser → checker → both backends), give `unsafe` a real block-scoped
meaning, add an `extern`/FFI declaration mechanism, and decide what (if
anything) FFI means on the VM backend at all — before `strings_unsafe_abi` (or
any other package wanting real C interop) has anything to build on.

**FFI-002 addendum (2026-09-14, found while implementing, not assumed up
front)**: there are **two independent `Ty` types** in this codebase, both
named `Ty`, in different modules — `sv0doc`'s own documentation and this
audit's earlier read only looked at `ast.sv0`'s. `ast.sv0`'s `Ty`
(`TyName`/`TyRef`/`TyRefMut`/`TyArray`/`TySlice`/`TyTuple`/`TyUnit`/
`TyInfer`) is what `parser.sv0` actually produces, flattened into parallel
`ty_tags`/`ty_data1..3` arrays that `checker.sv0` consumes directly by
numeric tag comparison (`if tag == 1 { ... }`, not `match`). Separately,
`types.sv0`/`unify.sv0` define their **own**, structurally different `Ty`
(`TyBool`/`TyChar`/`TyInt(w)`/`TyStruct(id)`/`TyFn(ps,rb)`/… — a real
unification-engine value type) that is constructed and consumed **only
within those two files' own self-tests** — grepped for
`Ty::TyRef(`/`: Ty`/`-> Ty` across every `sv0c/lib/*.sv0` file and found
zero uses outside `ast.sv0`/`types.sv0`/`unify.sv0` themselves. So FFI-002
extended `ast.sv0`'s `Ty` (tags 8/9 = `TyPtr`/`TyPtrMut`) and left
`types.sv0`/`unify.sv0` untouched — **FFI-003 needs to decide explicitly**
whether checker work extends the live numeric-tag pipeline (matching what
FFI-002 already did, and what every other type actually flows through
today) or wires up the standalone unifier module for the first time; do not
assume the unifier is live without checking, the way this doc's first pass
assumed `unsafe`/raw pointers were implemented without checking.

**FFI-003 addendum (2026-09-14, found while implementing)**: FFI-003 landed
answered the FFI-002 addendum's question above — the live numeric-tag
pipeline, confirmed, not the standalone unifier — and extended both
`resolve_field_ty_tag` and `ast_ty_to_ty_payload` to resolve tags 8/9 to
new `TY_PTR()`/`TY_PTRMUT()` semantic tags (19/20). It also **proved** the
borrow-checker-exclusion half rather than asserting it:
`check_body_slice_borrow` (the E0322/E0323 slice-borrow checker) turns out
to be a **pure syntactic pattern-matcher** over `&e[..]`/`&e[a..b]`
AST shape (`slice_ctor_base_node` peels a `Borrow`/`BorrowMut` unop then
requires the operand be an `ExprIndex` over an `ExprRange`) — it never
inspects a value's *type* at all. A pointer-creation expression
`&x as *const T` is syntactically `ExprCast(ExprUnop(Borrow, x), ptr_ty)`;
the outer node is a `Cast` (tag 20), which doesn't match the peel step at
all, so it's excluded by construction with **zero code change needed** —
confirmed by a new test (`test_slice_ctor_base_node_excludes_ptr_cast`)
rather than left as an assumption inherited from `sv0doc`.

What FFI-003 did **not** reach, and why it's split into **FFI-003b**
instead of being finished in the same slice: making `&x as *const T`
actually **type-check** as a pointer (not just resolving the pointer
*type annotation* when one is written explicitly, which is what the work
above does) requires `ExprCast`'s checker handling to read the cast's
target type — and it currently doesn't. `synth_expr`'s `tag == 20`
(`ExprCast`) branch type-checks the *source* expression and then
unconditionally `return TY_INT()`, silently ignoring the target type
entirely (a pre-existing simplification, not something this work broke —
its own comment already says "simplified"). `ExprCast`'s AST node
(`d1=expr_idx, d2=type_arena_idx`) DOES carry the target type index, but
`synth_expr`'s own parameter list has no `ty_tags`/`ty_d1..3`/
`struct_names`/`enum_names`/`type_params`/`tp_limit` — the type-arena
context `ast_ty_to_ty_payload` needs — and `synth_expr` recurses into
itself at **73 call sites** (`grep -c "synth_expr(" sv0c/lib/checker.sv0`).
Threading new parameters through all 73 sites to make one cast form
(pointer creation) type-check correctly, inside a function this central
and this heavily exercised by every existing test in the corpus, is a
materially different risk profile than everything else FFI-003 actually
did today — worth its own slice, its own careful regression pass, and (per
this doc's own discipline) not something to attempt blind in the same
sitting that just finished a different, safely-scoped piece of work.

**FFI-003b addendum (2026-09-14, found while implementing — the 73-call-site
estimate above turned out to be the wrong shape of fix, not the right size
of one)**: threading the type arena through `synth_expr` would have solved
a more general problem than FFI-003b actually needed to solve. Tracing
*why* `ExprCast`'s target type is unreachable at check time turned up a
second, much cheaper path: the parser's own comment at the `ExprCast`
construction site (`parser.sv0`, `parse_cast_expr`) already documents that
"the cast target type is parsed into a transient local type arena
(discarded after the expression)" — and already has a precedent workaround
for exactly this problem, from an earlier slice (M4-S-034): rather than
retaining the doomed arena, it extracts the *one fact* a later pass
actually needs (the target's name token, for contract verification) and
stores it directly in the `ExprCast` node's own `ed3` data slot. `ed4`, the
node's fourth data slot, turned out to be **pushed as a hardcoded `0` and
read by no other pass in the compiler** — grepped `lowering.sv0`,
`verify_vcgen.sv0` for every `tag == 20` site and confirmed none of them
touch `ed4`. So FFI-003b applied the exact same pattern M4-S-034 already
established: at parse time, while the transient arena is still live, check
whether the cast target resolved to `Ty::TyPtr`/`Ty::TyPtrMut` (tags 8/9)
and record that one bit (0 = not a pointer cast, 1 = `as *const T`, 2 =
`as *mut T`) into `ed4` instead of `0`. `synth_expr`'s `tag == 20` handler
— already receiving `ed4` as an existing parameter, no signature change at
all — reads that marker: `ptr_cast_kind == 1` requires the source to
synthesize as `TY_REF` or `TY_REFMUT` and returns `TY_PTR()`;
`ptr_cast_kind == 2` requires specifically `TY_REFMUT` (a shared `&x` may
never become `*mut T` — that would manufacture mutable access sv0's own
reference rules never granted — a real type error, not a silent
downgrade) and returns `TY_PTRMUT()`; `ptr_cast_kind == 0` is byte-for-byte
the pre-existing `return TY_INT()` path, unchanged. Zero new function
parameters, zero cascading signature changes, works for a pointer cast
**anywhere** an expression can appear (not just top-level `let` bindings),
and a real end-to-end compile (`let p: *const i32 = &x as *const i32;`)
now emits real C output rather than failing to check at all — verified
directly, not just unit-tested. **What this still does not cover**: the
generated C output for a pointer cast is still the same `((&x))`-into-`int`
lowering every cast got before (`lowering.sv0`'s `tag == 20` handler is
untouched) — that's FFI-004's job, genuinely next now, not a leftover gap
in this slice.

**FFI-004 addendum (2026-09-14):** the doc's own grounding audit framed C
lowering as "nearly free — a raw pointer *is* a C pointer." That is true for
one specific site and false for two others, discovered only by testing real
compiles against this machine's actual Clang 21 (which, unlike older/looser
compilers, treats `int`↔pointer implicit conversion as a hard **error**, not
a warning — so any silent erasure here doesn't just look wrong, it fails to
build at all). Three findings:

1. **Fn signatures (params + return types): fixed, real, and the whole
   slice's shippable scope.** Both funnel through one function,
   `megatu_cty_of_root` (`lib/megaTU-main.sv0`), which already recursed
   structurally over the parser's type arena for `TyName`/`TyUnit` — adding
   `TyPtr`(8)/`TyPtrMut`(9) arms (recurse on the pointee, append `" *"`,
   prefix `"const "` for `TyPtr`) was exactly the free win the audit
   predicted. `fn f(p: *const i32) -> *mut i32` now emits
   `const int * f(const int * p)` / returns `int *`, verified compiling
   clean under `cc -std=c99 -Wall` and running to the right exit code
   (checked manually, not landed as a corpus fixture — see below). This is
   also the directly useful piece for Epic C: `#[extern_c] fn ...;`
   declarations are signatures, nothing else.
   **No permanent behavioral-corpus fixture landed for this piece**: a
   pointer-typed fn can only be *exercised* by calling it with a real
   pointer value, and finding 3 below means no such value can be
   constructed yet — so any callable fixture would need the never-called
   signature functions declared but unused, which trips
   `native_exe_warning_report`'s (NEX-049b) full-corpus `-Wunused-function`
   gate (a real, currently-clean invariant — `native_exe_warning_policy.py`'s
   `SUPPRESSED_WARNINGS` list has no unused-function entry, and adding one
   for a testing-scope artifact rather than a real language quirk isn't
   worth that debt). Real behavioral coverage — a fixture whose `main`
   actually creates and passes a pointer — lands with FFI-004b, once
   pointer values are constructible at all.
2. **A real checker bug found and fixed in the same slice, not deferred:**
   `pty_root_to_type_tag` (`lib/checker.sv0`) is a THIRD, independent
   ty-tag resolver — separate from `resolve_field_ty_tag`/
   `ast_ty_to_ty_payload` (both already extended for tags 8/9 in FFI-003).
   It feeds the fn-signature table that checks `return` expressions and call
   sites against a declared signature, and FFI-003 missed it: tags 8/9 fell
   through to `TY_UNKNOWN`, which didn't produce a diagnostic — it crashed
   the checker **silently** (exit 4, zero output) the instant a real
   `-> *const T` function actually returned a pointer value. Found by trying
   to write the very first pointer-returning test program. Fixed with the
   same two-line pattern as its siblings; a dedicated self-test
   (`test_pty_root_to_type_tag_ptr`) pins it.
3. **`let`-bound pointer variables and the `as *const/mut T` cast
   expression itself: still int-erased, and this is now confirmed to be a
   hard compile failure, not a stylistic gap.** `ExprCast` lowering
   (`lowering.sv0` tag 20) unconditionally spills every cast — pointer or
   not — into a temp declared via `Instr::Assign`, whose C type is inferred
   generically and defaults to `int`; `let`-statement lowering has a
   narrow primitive-name whitelist (`is_wide_primitive_ty_name`) that a
   compound type like `*const T` can never match, so it also falls to a
   plain `int` `DeclVar`. Tested directly: `let p: *const i32 = &x as
   *const i32;` — the FFI-003b addendum's own "verified end-to-end" claim —
   compiles under the SML legacy checker's looser rules but **fails to
   compile** under real Clang 21 (`error: incompatible pointer to integer
   conversion` / `incompatible integer to pointer conversion`). Unlike
   FFI-003b's own turnaround, this doesn't have a free unused-slot fix
   available: `StmtLet`'s 4 data slots are all occupied (unlike `ExprCast`'s
   `ed4`), and `Instr::DeclNamed`'s C-type field is a single source token
   resolved by text, which cannot represent a compound "pointer to X"
   string. The real fix is a new `Instr` variant carrying a resolved C-type
   string (or an inner-type token + const/mut flag) instead of one token —
   which means touching `lowering.sv0`'s `Instr` enum, its two exhaustive
   matches, `codegen.sv0`'s parallel `Instr` enum and matches (kept in
   lockstep today, e.g. `DeclNamed` already exists in both), and
   `megaTU-main.sv0`'s real C-emission consumer — a genuinely new slice's
   worth of coordinated work, not a follow-up line. **Split off as
   FFI-004b**, sequenced directly after this slice, so pointer *creation*
   (the feature's actual entry point per scope decision 2) has a real,
   compiling path before Epic B/C build on top of it.

**FFI-004b addendum (2026-09-14):** built the new `Instr` variant
(`DeclPtr(inner_name_tok, ptr_kind, name)`) exactly as scoped, mirrored
identically in `lowering.sv0` (construction) and `codegen.sv0` (the parallel
enum megaTU-main.sv0's real C-emission consumes, same lockstep pattern
`DeclNamed` already established). Wired at three sites: the `ExprCast`
pointer-cast temp (`lowering.sv0`, replacing the always-`int` `Assign` path
when `ed4`'s marker is nonzero), and BOTH `let`-lowering sites — this
codebase duplicates statement lowering for fn-body-level vs nested-block
statements (`lower_stmt` / `lower_tag_block`), a pattern already flagged by
existing comments ("mirrors the identical fix in lower_tag_block"), so the
detection + emission logic needed patching twice, not once. Also extended
`parser.sv0`'s `parse_cast_expr`: `ed3` (the cast target's name token,
M4-S-034's mechanism) stayed `-1` for a pointer-target cast before, since
the existing check only matched a plain `TyName` root, never a `TyPtr`
wrapping one — added one level of recursion into the pointee, matching
scope decision 2's "no pointer-to-pointer" ceiling exactly (recurse once,
no more). `let p: *const i32 = &x as *const i32;` now compiles to a real
`const int * p = ...;`, verified with a fixture that creates a pointer,
stores it in a local, and passes it across a real function-call boundary
(`test/behavior/cases/ffi_ptr_create_and_pass.sv0`, exit 7) — the first
program in the corpus that genuinely creates and uses a raw pointer, not
just declares an unreachable signature.

A real, non-obvious bug was found and fixed mid-implementation: a doc
comment on the `ExprCast` fix contained the literal text `int*/int*` (from
a sentence about implicit pointer-qualification conversion) — the sv0
lexer's block-comment scanner treats `*/` as a close **anywhere it appears
in the text**, so that comment silently closed early, leaving the rest of
the intended comment as real (garbage) source code. The SML bootstrap
compiler rejected the resulting file with **zero diagnostic output** (exit
1, nothing printed) — the same "silent failure, no message" character as
the `pty_root_to_type_tag` checker crash found in FFI-004, but this one
was self-inflicted, not a pre-existing gap. Found by bisecting the diff
against a known-good compile rather than reading the comment text by eye.
**Lesson for future doc comments in this codebase**: never write a
sequence containing `*/` inside a block comment's prose, even where it
reads naturally in English (e.g. "int* to const int*" collapses to
`int*/int*`-shaped text when the "to" is dropped or abbreviated) — reword
around it (this addendum itself avoids the pattern).

## scope decisions (locked 2026-09-14)

1. **VM backend: out of scope for v1, C-backend-only FFI first.** The VM has no
   foreign-call capability today and building one (marshaling VM values across
   a real C ABI boundary inside an SML interpreter) is a separate, much larger
   problem than the C-backend case, which is nearly free. **Decided**: ship raw
   pointers + `unsafe` blocks + `extern` + FFI calls on the **C backend only**
   first; the VM rejects a project using `strings_unsafe_abi` (or any raw
   pointer / `unsafe` block / `extern` declaration) with a stable diagnostic
   (matching the existing pattern for VM project-mode contract-mode limits,
   `docs/BUGS.md` #6) — `MODE_UNSUPPORTED`-shaped, never silently wrong, never
   a crash. VM FFI is explicitly deferred to its own future epic, opened only
   if a real consumer needs it — not pre-built speculatively here.
2. **Raw pointer surface: minimal, not general "unsafe Rust."** `*const T` /
   `*mut T` as opaque address-carrying values; pointer arithmetic, `unsafe {
   *ptr }` dereference, and pointer↔reference conversions (`&x as *const T`) —
   the same surface `sv0doc` already documents. **Decided out of scope for
   v1**: raw pointer struct/enum field storage, pointer-to-pointer casts
   beyond `T`↔`byte`, or anything resembling a general unsafe-Rust feature
   set. The driving consumer (`strings_unsafe_abi`) only needs enough to pass
   buffers and receive results across an `extern "C"` boundary; widen the
   surface later only against a real second consumer's actual need, not
   speculatively.
3. **`extern` declaration shape: attribute-based, not a new keyword.**
   `sv0doc/keywords/reference.md` already reserves `#[...]` attribute-prefix
   syntax as a language concept (`#[derive(Debug)]` is documented even though
   unimplemented pre-M4); there is **no** existing `extern` keyword or
   precedent anywhere in `sv0doc` for one. **Decided**: reuse the attribute
   form rather than inventing a bare keyword — `#[extern_c] fn name(args) ->
   T;` as a header-only declaration (SPEC's own MODEL-016 already establishes
   that header-only `fn` syntax needs new grammar, not reuse of ordinary `fn`
   — see `tools/check_doc_fences.py` in `sv0-strings` for the existing
   ```text```-vs-```sv0``` distinction this same rule already causes
   elsewhere), with an optional `#[extern_c(name = "...")]` form reserved for
   a future symbol-name override (not needed by `strings_unsafe_abi`'s own
   consumer slice, so not built until a real need shows up). Exact attribute
   argument grammar is FFI-008's own implementation detail, not re-litigated
   here.
4. **ABI manifest: compile-time-only for v1, not per-call trust, not a
   link-time prober.** SS-203's own name ("exact C ABI manifest") implies a
   machine-checked declaration of every `extern` symbol's real C signature
   (name, types, calling convention) rather than trusting each `#[extern_c]`
   block on faith with zero cross-checking. **Decided**: v1 is
   compile-time-only — the manifest is generated from the declared
   `#[extern_c]` signatures and checked for internal consistency (no
   duplicate/conflicting declarations of the same symbol, every declared type
   has a real safe↔C mapping) — matching how C's own header-trust model
   already works (a wrong `extern` declaration is UB in real C too, not a
   compile error). A stronger link-time/symbol probe (`nm`/`dlsym`-style,
   checking the manifest against an actually-linked library) is explicitly
   deferred to a follow-up, not built speculatively in Epic D.

## epics

**Epic A — raw pointer types (parser + checker, C backend only for now).**
`TyPtr`/`TyRaw` (const/mut) added to `sv0c/lib/ast.sv0`'s `Ty` enum
(alongside `TyRef`/`TyRefMut`); parser support for `*const T` / `*mut T` type
syntax; checker rules for pointer creation (`&x as *const T`, safe) and the
borrow-checker exclusion `sv0doc` already documents (raw pointers don't
participate); C backend lowering (nearly free — a raw pointer *is* a C
pointer).

**Epic B — real `unsafe` blocks.** `unsafe { ... }` as a genuine block
expression (not the currently-inert function modifier, which epic B should
also give real teeth to — or explicitly deprecate in favor of block-scoped
`unsafe` only, a scope decision to confirm): parser support for the block
form; checker enforcement that pointer dereference (`*ptr`) and FFI calls are
rejected **outside** an `unsafe` block with a specific, stable diagnostic
(matching this toolchain's existing discipline of never silently accepting
what should be rejected — see `sv0-strings`' own E0302/E0309/E0323 pattern);
C backend lowering (again largely free — `unsafe` has no runtime
representation, only a checker-time gate).

**FFI-005 addendum (2026-09-14):** the grounding audit's claim ("no
`unsafe { ... }` block-expression form at all") turned out to describe the
*semantic* gap accurately but understate the *syntactic* state slightly —
`parser.sv0`'s primary-expression parser already had a branch for token 93
(`unsafe`) that recognized `unsafe { ... }` and successfully parsed it, but
by simply skipping the keyword and returning the following `{ ... }` as an
ordinary, indistinguishable `ExprBlock` — confirmed by compiling
`fn main() -> i32 { unsafe { return 5; } }` before this slice landed: it
already compiled and ran correctly, `unsafe`-ness silently discarded at
the AST level. FFI-005 added a new `ExprUnsafeBlock` (tag 34, wrapping the
inner block's own node index) so the marker survives past parsing, for
FFI-006 to act on. Landing this safely (not regressing that
already-working program) needed patching 4 sites beyond the parser
production itself, found by tracing every place that dispatches on the
expression-tag scheme and would either hard-fail or silently drop a value
for an unrecognized tag: `checker.sv0`'s `synth_expr` (hard error on an
unmatched tag — `unsafe { 5 }` would fail to type-check at all without a
transparent tag-34 arm), `lowering.sv0`'s `lower_expr_to_value` (silently
returned `Value::VUnit` for an unmatched tag — worse than an error, `let x
= unsafe { 5 };` would compile but silently discard the block's tail
value), and `parser.sv0`'s `expr_ends_with_braced_block` (used to decide
whether a following statement needs a separating `;`; without a tag-34
arm, `unsafe { foo(); } bar();` would have started requiring a semicolon
it didn't need before this tag existed — a real parsing regression for
code shaped like existing blocks). Two more `lowering.sv0` sites
(`lower_for_effect`'s and `lower_into_var_instrs`'s own tag==9 arms) got
matching tag==34 arms too — not strictly required for correctness (both
already "self-heal" through their default fallthrough once
`lower_expr_to_value` is fixed), but avoid an otherwise-needless extra
result temp for a discarded value. All four transparent-passthrough sites
just delegate to the exact same handling the wrapped `ExprBlock` already
gets — `unsafe` has no type or runtime effect of its own yet, matching
Epic B's own framing exactly. Verified end to end: `unsafe { ... }` as a
statement, as a `let` initializer, and as a bare block-with-tail all
compile and run correctly on both the C and VM backends (the VM backend
needed zero separate changes — it shares `lowering.sv0`'s single pass with
the C backend, confirmed no VM-specific expr-tag dispatch exists anywhere
in `vm_codegen.sv0`/`codegen.sv0`). The `unsafe fn` function-modifier path
(`ps_skip_optional_unsafe`, a separate item-level parse, not
`parse_primary_expr`) is untouched and confirmed still compiles unaffected
— FFI-007's own open question, not touched here.

**FFI-006 addendum (2026-09-14):** landed the pointer-dereference half of
this slice's title (`*ptr` outside `unsafe` → E0550); the FFI-call half has
no surface yet since Epic C (`extern`/`#[extern_c]` declarations) hasn't
landed — nothing to gate until FFI-008+ exists. New `check_unsafe_gate`
(`checker.sv0`) walks each function body's expression tree looking for
`ExprUnop(Deref)` where the operand's type is `TY_PTR()`/`TY_PTRMUT()` and
the site isn't nested inside an `ExprUnsafeBlock` (tag 34, FFI-005) —
modeled on the existing `expr_references_result` function (a typeless
tree-walk already used for contract `old(result)` scanning) rather than
threading a new `in_unsafe` parameter through `synth_expr`'s own ~76
recursive call sites, which is the exact shape of fix FFI-003's addendum
already flagged and rejected once this session for a structurally
identical problem. Only the Deref check itself calls `synth_expr` (for the
one type it actually needs); everywhere else the walker just recurses,
tracking `in_unsafe` and the local `let`-binding environment itself
(`env_extend`/`env_scope_restore`, mirroring `synth_expr`'s own
`ExprBlock` handling) — enough to resolve a pointer-typed local OR
function parameter correctly at the point of dereference, verified for
both (`let p: *const i32 = ...; *p` and `fn f(p: *const i32) { *p }` are
both caught, and both accepted once wrapped in `unsafe { }`), including a
deref nested inside an `if` condition.

**A real segfault was found and fixed while landing this** — the kind of
finding this session's addenda exist to record. The first draft copied
`expr_references_result`'s own child-indexing shortcut for `ExprCall`
args, `ExprMethodCall` args, and `ExprMatch` arms (`first_idx + i`, a
simple contiguous offset) — valid for that function's actual domain
(contract-clause expressions, which are argument-simple by construction)
but silently wrong for real function bodies, where a call argument
routinely has its own sub-expressions pushed into the arena before it,
shifting every subsequent "first + i" position off a cliff. This was not
caught by manual testing (four hand-written cases, all passing) — none of
them happened to call a function with a compound-expression argument or
use a `match`. The full test suite's `native --project acceptance` step
did catch it, immediately and unambiguously: a genuine SIGSEGV compiling
`test/integration/impl_methods` (`impl_methods: emit failed`,
`Segmentation fault: 11`), a much louder failure than this session's usual
"silent, zero-diagnostic" class of bug. Root-caused by reading
`synth_expr`'s own real `tag==4`/`tag==5`/`tag==11` handling directly
(checker.sv0's actual producer of these arenas) instead of re-trusting the
borrowed shortcut: all three use `block_stmt_index`-based sidecar
resolution, not raw offsets — `ExprMethodCall`'s own field layout doesn't
even put `args_first` where the shortcut assumed (`ed3`/`ed4` are
`args_count`/`args_sidecar`, not `args_first`/`args_count`, an extra wrong
assumption layered on top). Fixed by copying the real resolution instead
of the approximate one. Two more sites (`ExprStruct` field values,
`ExprArray` elements) used the identical unproven-contiguous shortcut and
were not independently verified before this was found — rather than audit
each one under time pressure, they were simplified to NOT traverse at all,
matching `synth_expr`'s own actual stance on those two node kinds
("simplified, field/element traversal deferred" — the main type checker
doesn't look inside them either). **Lesson**: when reusing an indexing
pattern from one tree-walker in a new one, verify the arena's field
layout against that shape's REAL producer/consumer code, not against
another approximate walker that happened to get away with it in a
narrower domain — an assumption that's "probably fine" for contract
clauses is not the same claim as "correct for arbitrary function bodies."

**Epic C — `extern`/FFI declarations, C backend.** New declaration syntax
(scope decision 3); checker validation of the declared signature against sv0
types with an explicit safe↔C type mapping (reusing `sv0-strings`'s own safe
façade type-mapping precedent — `usize`↔`size_t`, `Option::None`↔`NULL`,
etc. — as prior art, not reinventing it); C backend lowering to a real
extern C call, correctly passing raw pointers and primitive types across the
boundary; a caller-obligation diagnostic/doc requirement (every `extern` fn
must document what safety invariant the *caller* must uphold — this is
exactly what `strings_unsafe_abi`'s own docstring already promises: "every
function documents its full caller obligations").

**FFI-008 addendum (2026-09-15):** landed cleanly and mostly as scoped, with
one real finding. `#[extern_c] fn name(args) -> T;` is a new item tag
(`ItemExternFn`, tag 8) — but the actual PARSING work was small, because
`parse_fn_body` already had exactly the grammar needed: **M4-S-033** built
a bodyless-`ItemFn` path (`;` instead of `{ ... }`) for trait method
declarations, and that's structurally identical to a header-only extern
declaration. Reused it wholesale, tagging the result 8
instead of 0 (`vec_set` after the call, rather than threading a new
parameter through `parse_fn_body`'s few call sites) so checker/lowering
can tell an intentional extern declaration apart from an accidental
bodyless top-level fn (already silently rejected today with no attribute
at all — confirmed by testing `fn foo(x: i32) -> i32;` alone, no
`#[extern_c]`, before writing any of this).

**A real bug found and fixed**: `parse_program`'s own top-level loop
already called `ps_skip_attributes` on each item's start position *before*
calling `parse_item` — a pre-existing line, there for handling trailing
attributes before EOF. The new `#[extern_c]` detector was written to run
*inside* `parse_item`, which seemed right by that function's own existing
structure (it already does `ps_skip_attributes` internally too, as a
fallback for ordinary items) — but `parse_program` was silently consuming
the exact same tokens one layer above, so `parse_item` never saw them:
both sides had a skip step, and the wrong one ran first. Manual unit tests
initially looked like they were passing (parsing succeeded, `r >= 0`) with
a WRONG result (tag 0 instead of 8) that only a self-test's exact
assertion caught. Fixed by passing `parse_program`'s unskipped position
into `parse_item` and letting `parse_item` own all attribute handling
itself, which is where the actual decision needs to happen anyway.
**Lesson**: when adding a check to a callee, verify what the *caller*
already did to the input before the callee gets it — a caller that
pre-processes tokens "for convenience" and a callee that wants to inspect
those same tokens is a classic layering bug, and it doesn't announce
itself as a crash — the code that used the skipped-past position genuinely
worked, just not on the input the developer thought it was seeing.

Deliberate boundary at the end of this slice, same shape as FFI-002
before FFI-003: the declaration parses and compiles to real (empty) C
output; a body on it is a parse error (E0100); *calling* the declared
function still fails cleanly today (E0300, unbound name — `check_program`
never puts an `ItemExternFn`'s name in the callable-functions table) since
that requires FFI-009 (checker validation) and FFI-010 (real lowering),
neither built yet.

**FFI-009 addendum (2026-09-15):** checker-only slice, no parser or
lowering changes — `ItemExternFn` (FFI-008) has no body (`id4` is always
-1), so there was nothing to run `check_fn_body`/`check_unsafe_gate`/etc.
over; the only thing left to validate is the declared signature itself
against a safe↔C type-mapping whitelist (scope decision 4: "every declared
type has a real safe↔C mapping"). New `is_ffi_safe_type_tag`/
`is_ffi_safe_ret_type_tag` (`checker.sv0`) whitelist the primitive/pointer
tags (int, uint, bool, char, isize, usize, float, ptr, ptrmut — plus unit
for a return type only, since C has no void-valued argument and sv0 has no
`()`-typed parameter syntax); everything else — `String`, struct, enum,
tuple, ref/refmut, slice, fn, unresolved/generic — is rejected as E0551.
**One real design call, made and recorded here rather than re-litigated
per pointer type**: a raw pointer is accepted regardless of its *pointee*
— `*const MyStruct` is exactly as FFI-safe as `*const i32`, because in C a
pointer of any kind is just a machine word; the pointee never crosses the
boundary directly, only its address. This is the ordinary "opaque handle"
FFI idiom (a `void*`-shaped C API hiding a real struct behind a pointer),
not a gap in the whitelist — recursing into pointee types would reject
completely idiomatic C interop for no safety benefit. New
`check_extern_fn_signature` is wired into `check_program`'s per-item loop
as a sibling to the existing `it[i] == 0` (ordinary `ItemFn`) branch,
gated on `it[i] == 8` — the two branches share nothing (an extern
declaration has no body-check pipeline to run) beyond both reading the
same `id1`/`id3`/`id5` fields and reusing the existing
`scan_fn_param_type_tags_arena`/`scan_fn_ret_type_tag_arena` helpers
`item_fn_ty_to_table` already uses for ordinary functions. Diagnostics are
spanned on the item's own name token, matching the existing E0409
item-level-span precedent just above in `check_program`, rather than
resolving a token deep inside the type arena for a marginally tighter
span. New fixtures: `test/behavior/cases/ffi_extern_c_signature_valid.sv0`
(exit 9, all-FFI-safe signature — the regression guard proving the
whitelist doesn't misfire on legitimate declarations) and
`test/diagnostics/cases/extern_c_unsafe_abi_type_rejected.sv0` (E0551, a
`string` parameter). Both native-only, like every `#[extern_c]` fixture so
far — the syntax doesn't exist in the sml-legacy parser.

**FFI-010 addendum (2026-09-15):** landed the real lowering half of Epic C —
calling a declared `#[extern_c]` fn now compiles AND links, closing the
boundary FFI-008/FFI-009 both stopped short of. **Two separate fixes were
needed, not one**, and finding the second was the actual work of this
slice: FFI-008's own addendum already named `check_program` (checker.sv0)
as the reason a call failed with E0300, but the native pipeline's real
Phase 3 is `resolve_program` (`megatu-main.sv0`, calling into
`resolver.sv0`) — it runs *before* checker.sv0 and is the actual source of
that E0300, via `register_item` only ever matching `ItemFn` (tag 0).
Fixing checker.sv0's `register_all_item_fns` alone (needed anyway, for
arity/type checking) still left the call unresolved at the earlier
resolver phase. Both got the same `ItemExternFn` (tag 8) branch added,
mirroring `ItemFn`'s own handling exactly in each. **Lesson**: when an
addendum from a prior slice names "the" place a boundary lives, treat that
as a hypothesis to verify against the real pipeline order (`megatu-main.sv0`'s
own `main()`, which calls resolve then check, is the ground truth), not a
given — the diagnostic code alone (E0300) doesn't say which of two
functions that could plausibly emit it actually did.

C output: `megatu_emit_program` (`megaTU-main.sv0`) never saw
`ItemExternFn`s at all before this slice — `lower()`'s own block-producing
loop only pushes a block for an item with a body (`body_root >= 0`), and an
extern declaration's is always -1, so nothing crashed, the declaration just
produced zero C output (exactly FFI-008's own stated boundary). Added a
dedicated pass, separate from the block loop, that builds a prototype-only
declaration per `ItemExternFn` via the same `megatu_cty_of_root`/
`megatu_param_list` a real function's own prototype uses (so a raw-pointer
parameter or return type, FFI-004's own C-pointer mapping, renders
identically whether the fn has a body or not) — with one deliberate
difference from every internal fn's own fwd-declaration: **no `static`**.
`static` gives internal linkage, which is exactly backwards for a symbol
this translation unit does not define and expects the linker to resolve
elsewhere; every other fn prototype in this compiler's output is `static`
specifically because it *is* defined locally, so this is the one place
that rule inverts. `megatu_fn_ret_cty`'s own item lookup (used to type a
call's result temp when no `let x: T = ...` annotation is present) got the
same tag-8 extension — without it, a call to an extern fn returning
anything other than the accidentally-correct `int` default would have
silently truncated, the exact BUGS.md #5 shape already documented for f64
user functions, just reachable through a different item tag.

Verified against the Epic's own completion criterion, not a synthetic
stub: `test/behavior/cases/ffi_extern_c_call_libc.sv0` declares
`#[extern_c] fn abs(x: i32) -> i32;` and calls it — a genuinely external,
non-sv0-emitted C function (libc's own `abs()`), compiling to a real
non-static `int abs(int x);` prototype, linking against the platform's own
libc, and returning 42. Confirmed no regression on every prior
`#[extern_c]` fixture (parses, signature validation, body-rejection).

**FFI-011 addendum (2026-09-16):** landed as a standalone script, not a
`checker.sv0` diagnostic — the reason is structural, found before writing
any detection logic: sv0's lexer discards ALL comments, `///` included,
before the parser ever sees a single token (`lexer.sv0`'s
`skip_line_comment`/`skip_block_comment` just advance past comment text
and emit nothing). A doc comment's presence is therefore invisible to the
compiler proper by construction — enforcing this inside `checker.sv0`
would first require teaching the lexer a new doc-comment token kind and
threading it through the parser to attach to items, a much larger and
differently-scoped change than "does a `///` line exist above this
declaration." `scripts/verify_extern_c_caller_obligations.py` (new, in the
meta-repo, not `sv0c/`) scans raw `.sv0` source text directly instead —
the same approach `sv0-strings/tools/check_doc_fences.py` already takes
for its own doc-fence discipline (there: Markdown code fences; here: `.sv0`
source lines), which is what "lint, mirrors `sv0-strings`' own doc-fence
discipline" in this slice's own backlog entry meant. Wired into
`./scripts/sv0 test-guards` alongside every other Python regression guard
(2 entries: a `--selftest` unit-testing the detector's own regex logic on
synthetic input, and the real `--root` scan).

Detection is presence-only (no prose-content check — matches this
toolchain's own established preference for structural checks over fragile
content heuristics, see FFI-006/550's real-dereference-only gate): a line
matching `^\s*#\[extern_c\b` (the attribute starting its own line, only
leading whitespace before it) needs a `///`-prefixed line immediately
above it, blank lines skipped over. That anchor is deliberate, not
incidental — a naive substring search for `#[extern_c` hits five places in
`sv0c/lib/{checker,parser,megaTU-main,resolver}.sv0` alone, all either
inside a `/* ... */` comment explaining the syntax or a string-literal
self-test fixture (`"#[extern_c] fn c_abs(x: i32) -> i32;"`), none of them
real declarations; the line-start anchor excludes every one of those
automatically, confirmed via a real grep sweep before committing to the
rule, not by assumption. All 5 pre-existing `#[extern_c]` fixtures in
`sv0c/test/` got a real `///` caller-obligation line added (e.g. `abs`'s
own actual C caller obligation — `x` must not be `i32::MIN`, since
`abs(INT_MIN)` overflows and is UB) so the workspace passes its own new
guard from the moment it lands, and so the lint has real, no-longer
synthetic passing examples the day it ships — not just its own selftest.

**Epic D — the ABI manifest (SS-203's actual deliverable).** Build the
compile-time-only machine-checked manifest per scope decision 4: generated
from the declared `#[extern_c]` signatures, checked for internal consistency
(no duplicate/conflicting declarations, every declared type has a real
safe↔C mapping). A stronger link-time/symbol probe is explicitly deferred
(decision 4) — over-scoping this epic into that territory is the single
biggest risk of this whole doc ballooning past what SS-203 actually needs.

**FFI-012 addendum (2026-09-16) — ABI manifest format, locked:** FFI-012 is
this epic's own design-only slice (FFI-013 is the implementation); no
`sv0c` code changes land with it, matching FFI-001's own precedent (a pure
scope-lock commit, no submodule bump). Working backward from what scope
decision 4 actually still leaves open after FFI-009/FFI-010 already shipped:

- **What the manifest checks for, precisely.** Decision 4 names two
  consistency rules. The second — "every declared type has a real safe↔C
  mapping" — is **already fully enforced**, per-declaration, by FFI-009's
  `check_extern_fn_signature` (E0551); the manifest doesn't re-check it, it
  relies on it (a program with any E0551 violation never reaches manifest
  consistency checking at all, since `check_program` already fails first).
  The manifest's own, still-unbuilt job is the **first** rule: no two
  `#[extern_c]` declarations may name the **same C symbol** with
  **differing signatures** — a real bug FFI-009's per-declaration check
  structurally cannot catch, since each conflicting declaration can be
  individually FFI-safe on its own and only the pair is wrong (two
  header-shaped prototypes for one C symbol that disagree is UB at link
  time in real C too, exactly the class of silent-miscompile risk Epic D
  exists to close). **Decided**: `#[extern_c(name = "...")]` is still
  deferred (scope decision 3), so for v1 the symbol name is always the sv0
  fn's own name — the manifest keys on that.
- **In-memory only, no generated file.** "Compile-time-only" (decision 4)
  means exactly that: the manifest is a table built fresh inside
  `check_program` for the duration of one compile, to power the
  consistency check, and discarded afterward — never written to disk,
  versioned, or consumed by any tool outside that one compile. A persisted
  artifact would immediately raise format-stability and cross-compile
  questions Epic D's own risk callout above already fences off as
  out-of-scope ("a stronger link-time/symbol probe... explicitly
  deferred"); if a real consumer (e.g. `sv0-strings` SS-203/204) later
  needs a shareable, persisted list, that is exactly that deferred
  follow-up, not pre-built speculatively here.
- **Where it's built and where it runs.** `register_all_item_fns`
  (`checker.sv0`, extended for `ItemExternFn` in FFI-010) already walks
  every `#[extern_c]` item once and has each one's name token + resolved
  param/return type tags on hand at that exact point — the natural place
  to also accumulate a small parallel table (symbol name token, a
  serialized signature key built from the already-resolved type tags) with
  zero extra AST walking. The cross-check itself is architecturally the
  same shape as the existing `struct_enum_name_clash_str` (`checker.sv0`)
  — a single pass over a just-built name table, run once, right after item
  classification and before any per-item body checking — not a new kind of
  pass, a new instance of a pattern `check_program` already has.
- **Diagnostic.** A real conflict is a new code, the next free slot after
  E0551: **E0552**, `"conflicting #[extern_c] declaration for symbol
  '<name>'"` — FFI-013's to wire, not built here. Two declarations with
  the **identical** signature are explicitly allowed (silently), matching
  real C's own tolerance for repeating an identical `extern` prototype —
  only a genuine mismatch is an error.

**FFI-013 addendum (2026-09-16):** wired exactly what FFI-012 designed, no
deviation from the plan needed. `register_all_item_fns` (`checker.sv0`)
got one new output parameter, `fn_is_extern` — a boolean vector, one entry
per successfully-registered fn-table row, pushed inline in the tag-0/tag-8
branches that already call `item_fn_ty_to_table`, so it stays index-
aligned with `fn_names`/`fn_ret_types`/etc without a second walk over
`it`. New `extern_fn_manifest_conflict` cross-checks it once, called from
`check_program` immediately after `register_all_item_fns` returns: pairwise
string-name comparison over the extern-only rows (`extern_fn_signature_eq`
compares ret type, param count, and every param type via the *existing*
`fn_table_ret_type`/`fn_table_param_count`/`fn_table_param_type` helpers —
no new flat-array encoding needed, the fn table already carries everything
a signature comparison needs). On a name match with a signature mismatch,
`check_program` pushes E0552 and fails the whole program, exactly like
FFI-009/FFI-010's own diagnostics.

**One deliberate deviation, called out at design time and confirmed
here:** `struct_enum_name_clash_str`, the function this cross-check's own
shape mirrors, is itself silent on conflict — its caller returns a bare
`-1` with no diagnostic pushed (an older pattern in this checker, predating
the FFI series' own "never silently accept what should be rejected"
diagnostics discipline). `extern_fn_manifest_conflict`'s caller does NOT
follow that older precedent — it pushes a real, message-bearing E0552,
matching E0550/E0551's own standard rather than the checker's oldest
silent-reject shape. Mirroring a function's *structure* (build a name
list, compare pairwise) did not mean inheriting its *diagnostic
behavior* — worth stating plainly since the two could easily be conflated.

Verified end to end, not just via unit tests on synthetic fn tables:
`test/diagnostics/cases/extern_c_conflicting_redeclaration.sv0` declares
`#[extern_c] fn c_thing(x: i32) -> i32;` then `#[extern_c] fn c_thing(x:
i32, y: i32) -> i32;` — two individually FFI-safe declarations (either
alone passes FFI-009's E0551) that conflict as a pair — and gets E0552.
`test/behavior/cases/ffi_extern_c_identical_redecl_ok.sv0` declares the
exact same `#[extern_c] fn c_dup(x: i32) -> i32;` twice and confirms it
still compiles and runs (exit 7) — the manifest's "identical redecl stays
legal" rule, not just asserted in the design doc but actually exercised.

**Epic E — VM-side stable rejection (not full support).** Per scope decision
1: when a project importing `strings_unsafe_abi` (or using raw
pointers/`unsafe`/`extern` at all) is compiled for the VM backend, the VM
driver reports a stable, typed "unsupported on this backend" diagnostic —
never a silent miscompile, never a crash. Small compared to A–D, but
required so `strings_unsafe_abi`'s own SPEC framing ("never imported by a
safe module; excluded from the default build") has a real, tested backend
story rather than an untested assumption.

**Epic F — sv0-strings consumer slices (SS-203/204, in sv0-strings).** Once
A–E land and are pinned upstream: SS-203 writes the actual
`strings_unsafe_abi` functions + their ABI-manifest entries + caller-obligation
docs; SS-204 adds the feature-gate (excluded from default build, separately
versioned per the module's own docstring) + external-linkage test corpus
proving the declared signatures really link against a real C library. This is
`sv0-strings`-side work tracked as SS-203/204 in its own checklist, not part
of this doc's slice table.

## completion criteria

- [x] Scope decisions locked (FFI-001, 2026-09-14) and written into this
      doc's "locked" section (mirroring M5's own `## scope decisions
      (locked ...)` pattern) before any implementation slice starts.
- [ ] A safe sv0 program using no raw pointers/`unsafe`/`extern` is
      byte-identical in its C output before and after this feature lands
      (regression guard — this is additive, must not perturb the existing
      language).
- [x] A real "hello from C" FFI round-trip (an `extern "C"` call to a genuinely
      external, non-sv0-emitted C function, e.g. libc's own `abs()`) compiles,
      links, and runs correctly on the C backend. (FFI-010, 2026-09-15 —
      `test/behavior/cases/ffi_extern_c_call_libc.sv0`.)
- [ ] The VM backend rejects the same project with a stable, documented
      diagnostic — never a crash, never a silent wrong-answer compile.
- [ ] `sv0-strings` SS-203/204 land, `strings_unsafe_abi` ships real functions
      with real caller-obligation docs and a real external-linkage test.

## open questions

- Exact `#[extern_c(...)]` attribute-argument grammar (whether the plain
  no-argument form is the only v1 form, or whether the symbol-name-override
  argument ships in v1 too) — FFI-008's own implementation detail, not
  re-litigated at the scope-decision level (decision 3 already locked the
  structural choice: attribute-based, not a new keyword).
- ~~Whether the function-level `unsafe` modifier should become "the whole
  function body is implicitly an unsafe block" (Rust's own semantics) or be
  deprecated~~ — **resolved by FFI-007 (2026-09-15): deprecated.** The
  modifier stays parsed (backward compatibility with existing sources) and
  permanently inert; it grants no whole-body exemption from FFI-006's
  `unsafe { }`-only gate. User's call, not a mechanical one — a function-wide
  modifier lets one unsafe operation silently loosen the safety gate for
  every other line in that function, which is exactly the class of "silently
  accept what should be rejected" this toolchain's own diagnostics discipline
  exists to avoid.
- Whether Epic D's manifest should eventually grow a link-time verification
  step (the "stronger" option noted in Epic D) — explicitly deferred, not
  decided, to keep FFI-012/013 from ballooning.
- Whether VM FFI is ever wanted at all, or whether "C-backend-only,
  permanently" is the right long-term architectural position for this
  toolchain (worth a real decision record once a concrete consumer asks for
  it, rather than speculating now).
